title: Given an array of numbers and a target, find all unique quadruplets that add up to the target. (LeetCode: 4Sum)

s1_definition.profdef: The 4Sum problem finds all unique quadruplets summing to a target by extending the 3Sum pattern with one more fixed level: sort the array, use two nested loops to fix the first two elements, and apply a two-pointer scan for the remaining two. Duplicate skipping is applied at all four levels, yielding an n-cubed time solution.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh needs every unique group of four transaction amounts that together hit an exact target obligation. He sorts the amounts, then fixes the first amount with one loop and the second amount with an inner loop, and for each fixed pair Priya uses the two-pointer sweep to find the last two amounts that complete the target. He skips repeats at each of the four picking stages so no quadruple is reported twice.
s1_definition.oneliner: 4Sum is 3Sum with one extra fixed loop on top: fix two, two-pointer the rest, skip duplicates everywhere.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The 4Sum problem finds all unique quadruplets summing to a target by extending the 3Sum pattern with one more fixed level: sort the array, use two nested loops to fix the first two elements, and apply a two-pointer scan for the remaining two. Duplicate skipping is applied at all four levels, yielding an n-cubed time solution.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh needs every unique group of four transaction amounts that together hit an exact target obligation. He sorts the amounts, then fixes the first amount with one loop and the second amount with an inner loop, and for each fixed pair Priya uses the two-pointer sweep to find the last two amounts that complete the target. He skips repeats at each of the four picking stages so no quadruple is reported twice.

**One line to remember:** 4Sum is 3Sum with one extra fixed loop on top: fix two, two-pointer the rest, skip duplicates everywhere.

sections.s2_technical:
4Sum builds directly on 3Sum. We sort the array, then use an outer loop to fix the first element at index `i` and an inner loop to fix the second element at index `j` greater than `i`. For each fixed pair we run a two-pointer scan with `left = j + 1` and `right = end`, looking for two more values that make the total equal to the target.

At each level we skip duplicates. For the outer index `i`, if it equals the previous value we skip it. For the inner index `j`, if it equals the previous value within this `i` iteration we skip it. After recording a quadruplet, we advance `left` past repeated values and retreat `right` past repeated values. These four skips ensure every quadruplet is unique.

A finance usage example: suppose sorted amounts are `[1, 0, -1, 0, -2, 2]` sorted to `[-2, -1, 0, 0, 1, 2]` and the target is 0. Fixing -2 and -1, we need two values summing to 3; left at 0, right at 2 gives 2, too small, move left, and eventually we find combinations. Fixing -2 and 0, we need two summing to 2, and 0 and 2 works giving `[-2, 0, 0, 2]`. Continuing yields the complete set of unique quadruplets such as `[-2, -1, 1, 2]`, `[-2, 0, 0, 2]`, and `[-1, 0, 0, 1]`.

The senior-level nuance: watch for integer overflow when summing four values near the limits of the numeric range, so using a wider type for the running sum is prudent. The same template generalizes to k-sum: recursively fix elements and reduce the dimension by one until you reach the two-pointer base case, which turns the time complexity into n to the power of k minus one. Sorting once up front is essential for both the two-pointer squeeze and the clean duplicate handling, which is why this approach is preferred over a set-based deduplication.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's reconciliation team investigates cases where exactly four transaction amounts combine to an exact target figure, which can indicate a structured transaction split across four legs. They need every unique group of four amounts that sums to the target so each case can be reviewed. Checking every possible quadruple over a long list is quartic, which is hopeless for real volumes.

Problem 2 — Amounts repeat, and the investigation report must list each qualifying quadruple only once, so the solution must skip duplicate values carefully at all four selection levels.

The code defines a `QuadrupleFinder` class with a `findQuadruplets` method that sorts the amounts, fixes the first two with nested loops, applies a two-pointer scan for the last two, and skips duplicates at every level. A runnable demo seeds amounts and a target and logs every unique quadruplet.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the amounts `[1, 0, -1, 0, -2, 2]` and the target `0`.

Step 1: The finder sorts the amounts to `[-2, -1, 0, 0, 1, 2]`. Sorting groups duplicates and enables both the two-pointer squeeze and clean skipping.

Step 2: The outer loop fixes -2 at index 0. The inner loop fixes -1 at index 1. The two-pointer scan looks for two values summing to 3. Left at index 2 (value 0) and right at index 5 (value 2) give 2, too small, left moves right; eventually left at 1 and right at 2 give the pair completing `[-2, -1, 1, 2]`, which is recorded.

Step 3: Still fixing -2, the inner loop moves to the first 0 at index 2. The scan looks for two values summing to 2, and 0 at index 3 with 2 at index 5 gives the pair, so `[-2, 0, 0, 2]` is recorded. The second 0 as an inner anchor is skipped as a duplicate.

Step 4: The outer loop moves to -1 at index 1. The inner loop fixes the first 0. The scan looks for two values summing to 1, and 0 with 1 gives the pair, so `[-1, 0, 0, 1]` is recorded.

Step 5: Remaining anchors either duplicate earlier ones or cannot complete the target, so the scan ends. The three unique quadruplets have been collected.

Final output:

```
Oct 27, 2026 6:30:00 PM com.bank.recon.QuadrupleDemo main
INFO: Found 3 quadruplet(s): [[-2, -1, 1, 2], [-2, 0, 0, 2], [-1, 0, 0, 1]]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The 4Sum problem asks me to find every unique group of four numbers that adds up to a target, and the cleanest way to see it is as 3Sum with one extra fixed level stacked on top. I sort the array once, then use two nested loops to fix the first and second elements, and for each fixed pair I run the familiar two-pointer scan over the rest to find the remaining two elements that complete the target.

Duplicate handling happens at all four selection levels. At the outermost loop I skip a first element equal to the previous one, at the inner loop I skip a second element equal to the previous one within that iteration, and after recording a quadruplet I advance the left pointer past repeated values and retreat the right pointer past repeated values. Those four skips guarantee that every quadruplet I report is unique without my having to store and deduplicate results in a set.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in reconciliation to detect structured transactions. We investigated cases where exactly four transaction amounts combined to an exact target figure, which sometimes indicated a single payment deliberately split across four legs, and we needed every unique quadruple so each case could be reviewed. A quartic brute-force check was impossible at our volumes, so the sorted, nested-fix, two-pointer approach found the quadruplets efficiently.

The senior-level point I make is twofold. First, when summing four values I use a wider numeric type for the running sum to avoid integer overflow near the limits of the range. Second, this same skeleton generalizes to the general k-sum problem: I recursively fix elements and reduce the dimension by one until I reach the two-pointer base case, which gives a time complexity of n to the power of k minus one. Recognizing that 3Sum, 4Sum, and k-sum are all the same idea at different depths is what lets me solve any of them confidently from the same mental template.
